new_statements.quote: Metrically, iambs are assigned left-to-right, with final trochaic reversal. [...] High tones appear by default on the penultimate syllable regardless of vowel length. We derive this pattern by making three assumptions: first, when the left-to-right iambic parse leaves two short vowels at the right edge, they are footed into a trochee (trochaic reversal). Second, we assume that the last foot of the word is the head foot of the word, and third, that a High tone is assigned to the head syllable of the head foot of the word. The combination of trochaic reversal and right-headedness together ensure that the penult is the head of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Feet are iambs built left to right: even-numbered non-final vowels are rhythmically lengthened (lexically long vowels always head a foot and restart the count; long vowels are shortened phrase-finally). If two short syllables remain at the right edge they form a trochee; otherwise a single leftover final syllable is unparsed. The rightmost foot is the head foot, so in a word in isolation the primary stress is always the penult, which carries a default High tone; the lengthened even-numbered syllables to its left are secondary (foot-head) stresses. In multi-word phonological phrases the phrase is left-headed: the primary stress of the phrase is the primary stress of the first word, non-initial words lose their tone, and the single High tone is realized at the right end of a domain running from that stressed syllable up to (not including) the next foot head, so the pitch peak can sit up to three syllables after the stressed syllable ('incoherent' stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: heads of the non-final iambs, i.e. rhythmically lengthened even-numbered syllables counted from the left (and any lexically long vowel), e.g. [(ala:)(makí:)lɨ] 's/he fell', [(tʃiha:)(lama:)(kílɨ)] 'we fell' (§1, §3.1, Table 1).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically long vowels (a minority of roots, 17/59 verb roots) disrupt the iambic count but not the penult primary stress; nouns, adjectives and postpositions (not verbs) may bear lexical High tone on the final or antepenultimate syllable, which replaces the default penult tone in isolation (e.g. [(takí)] 'cricket', [(á:)(dʒahi)] 'potoo'; 72% of 119 personal names have final lexical tone; Portuguese loans keep tone on the Portuguese stressed syllable); monosyllables keep long vowels ([(í:)] 'tree'); phrase-medially a word-initial onsetless short vowel is left unparsed, shifting the count; vocatives shift final tone leftward and echo questions add a final H, so root-final lexical tone on common nouns varies between [(táki)] and [(takí)] in citation forms (§5, §7).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is for words in isolation (= one-word phonological phrases, citation forms); primary stress defined as head of the head (final) foot. In multi-word phrases only the first word keeps its tone and the H peak may be displaced rightward from the stressed syllable; vowel-length (footing) evidence for stress remains word-internal. Data from original fieldwork with two Kuikuro-speaking coauthors (Ipatse village variety).
new_statements.identity_note: Becker et al. 2025 describe the Kuikuro variety (Ipatse and neighbouring villages) of what Franchetto treats as one Upper Xingu Carib language with two dialects, Kuikuro/Matipu vs Kalapalo/Nahukwá; Glottolog kuik1246 'Kuikúro-Kalapálo' covers both. The stress statement should be attributed to the Kuikuro dialect only: Becker et al. say the Kalapalo foot type is 'unknown, but.. suggests that it is iambic', and Silva & Franchetto 2011 show Kalapalo phrase-level prominence patterns differ from Kuikuro's.

sources.quote: Metrically, iambs are assigned left-to-right, with final trochaic reversal. [...] High tones appear by default on the penultimate syllable regardless of vowel length. We derive this pattern by making three assumptions: first, when the left-to-right iambic parse leaves two short vowels at the right edge, they are footed into a trochee (trochaic reversal). Second, we assume that the last foot of the word is the head foot of the word, and third, that a High tone is assigned to the head syllable of the head foot of the word. The combination of trochaic reversal and right-headedness together ensure that the penult is the head of the word.
sources.locator: Abstract (first sentence quoted) and §3.1 'Default and lexical length in verbs', paragraph following Table 2 (author PDF pp. 1 and 7; journal pagination 2363-2393 not printed in the author PDF); restated in §3.6 'Local summary' and §7 'Conclusions'.
sources.note: Full word- and phrase-level analysis: left-to-right iambs with rhythmic lengthening of even-numbered vowels, lexical long vowels disrupt the count, final long vowels banned phrase-finally, final trochaic reversal; last foot is the head foot, so the penult of a word in isolation is uniformly the primary stress and carries a default High tone; in phrases the H-tone domain starts at the primary stress of the first word and may surface up to three syllables to the right ('incoherent' stress). Nouns/adjectives/postpositions may carry lexical tone (final or antepenult); verbs do not.

sources.note: Acoustic study of phrase-level prominence only (argument+head merges): in Kuikuro F0 is the correlate and 'the syllable that is perceived as prominent is always the last of the internal argument which immediately precedes the verb' (p.46); Kalapalo uses F0 merge-initially and duration elsewhere. No rule for stress in isolated words; Becker et al. 2025 note it did not track vowel length.
